chunks: Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father, from Ibn Mahboub, from Abdullah ibn Sinan, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), who said:
The thief, when he comes from his own self, repentant to Allah, Mighty and Majestic, and returns the stolen goods to its owner, so there is not cutting (of the hand) upon him.
ai.seo_question: When is a thief exempt from hand amputation in Shia jurisprudence?
ai.summary: In Shia jurisprudence, this hadith from Al-Kafi establishes that voluntary repentance (tawbah) combined with the restitution of the stolen goods nullifies the fixed hadd penalty of hand amputation. This ruling highlights the juristic principle that the primary purpose of the hadd is often retribution and deterrence, which are satisfied when the thief personally acknowledges the fault and restores the owner's right without needing a formal judicial trial. It underscores the Shia emphasis on the thief's internal state and direct action in mitigating divine punishment.

en.hubeali:
Ali Bin Ibrahim, from his father, from Ibn Mahboub, from Abdullah Bin Sinan, 
(It has been narrated) from Abu Abdullah<sup>asws</sup> having said:
‘The thief, when he comes from his own self, repentant to Allah<sup>azwj</sup> Mighty and Majestic, and returns the stolen goods to its owner, so there is not cutting (of the hand) upon him’.
